title: read_parquet(col_select = ...) sometime corrupts NA values
description:
As in the title, using `col_select` to select a column that contains `NA` returns corrupt data in some cases. A reprex is included, demonstrating the issue in one particular case. Additional debugging analysis was done by Claude, see following description:

`When a selected column lands at a different position in the result than it occupies in the file, the null mask is never applied: the non-null values are packed to the front and the tail is whatever was in the buffer. Usually zeros, occasionally not – one run gave me 7.7e+218 in the middle of the column. Row alignment against every other column is destroyed at the same time.`


``` r
# Package nanoparquet version 0.5.1.9000
# Important that the tibble have multiple columns
# Somehow the issue was not present if the first column had an NA in the same place
#df <- tibble::tibble(a = c(1, NA), b = c(2, NA))

# But this tibble reliably reproduces it
df <- tibble::tibble(a = 1:3, b = c(11, NA, 33))
f <- tempfile()
df |> nanoparquet::write_parquet(f)

# File contents
nanoparquet::read_parquet(f)
#> # A data frame: 3 × 2
#>       a     b
#>   <int> <dbl>
#> 1     1    11
#> 2     2    NA
#> 3     3    33

# Fetching the columns in order with col_select works correctly
nanoparquet::read_parquet(f, col_select = c("a", "b"))
#> # A data frame: 3 × 2
#>       a     b
#>   <int> <dbl>
#> 1     1    11
#> 2     2    NA
#> 3     3    33

# Fetching the columns out of order returns corrupt data,
# zero or close to it, and row order messed up
nanoparquet::read_parquet(f, col_select = c("b", "a"))
#> # A data frame: 3 × 2
#>           b     a
#>       <dbl> <int>
#> 1 1.1 e+  1     1
#> 2 3.3 e+  1     2
#> 3 4.94e-320     3
```

title: Constant POSIXct column gets seconds-scale min/max in footer statistics
description:
When a parquet file is written with `write_parquet()` and a `POSIXct` column is **constant** (all values identical), the min/max statistics in the file footer are written in seconds since the epoch, while the column is declared `TIMESTAMP(MICROS, true)` and the data pages correctly hold microseconds. 

```r
library(nanoparquet)

df <- data.frame(ts = as.POSIXct("2008-04-29 22:00:00", tz = "UTC") + rep(0, 16))
write_parquet(df, "/tmp/ts_const.parquet")
```

The data values are correct — `read_parquet()` returns `2008-04-29 22:00:00 UTC`, i.e. the pages store `1209506400000000` micros. But the footer says:

```
Int64({min: Some(1209506400), max: Some(1209506400), ...})
```

`1209506400` is the same instant in **seconds** — the conversion to micros was skipped on this code path.

The statistics are correct for non-constant columns, and for constant numeric and Date columns are also fine.

One way to inspect the statistics from Python:

```python
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
pq.read_metadata("/tmp/ts_const.parquet").row_group(0).column(0).statistics
# min/max are 1209506400 (seconds), should be 1209506400000000 (micros)
```

title: Read multiple parquet files (hive partitioning)
description:
I had a situation where I had hive-partitioned parquet files (exported from python Polars), the total number of rows is ~12M so it fits in memory, and I did not want to depend on DuckDB. I wanted to see if I could read it in with `nanoparquet`.

The data folder looks like this, with potentially more files in each subfolder:

```
disease_database_v1.0/
├── disease=cholera/
│   └── 00000000.parquet
├── disease=diphteria/
│   └── 00000000.parquet
├── disease=dysentery/
│   └── 00000000.parquet
├── disease=influenza/
│   └── 00000000.parquet
├── disease=malaria/
│   └── 00000000.parquet
├── disease=measles/
│   └── 00000000.parquet
├── disease=scarletfever/
│   └── 00000000.parquet
├── disease=smallpox/
│   └── 00000000.parquet
├── disease=tuberculosis/
│   └── 00000000.parquet
└── disease=typhus/
    └── 00000000.parquet
```

It would be nice to support multiple files (through globbing) in `read_parquet()`, or even better: hive partitioning with a potential filter on the partitioning variables so you only read the correct files?

Something like: 
```R
# glob
df <- read_parquet("disease_database_v1.0/**/*.parquet")

# or even something like this (although this filtering interface is very weird)
df <- read_parquet("disease_database_v1.0/**/*.parquet", hive_filter = disease == "cholera")
```


## Workaround
If someone stumbles upon this issue, I made a (naïve and inefficient) function as a "workaround" for this situation:

```R
read_parquet_glob <- function(fp, col_select = NULL, options = parquet_options()) {
  # get files
  pq_files <- Sys.glob(fp)
  
  # check if schemas are identical
  schemas <- lapply(pq_files, \(x) read_parquet_schema(x)[,-1])
  errmsg  <- "Schemas of partitioned files do not match."
  schema  <- Reduce(\(x, y) if (identical(x, y)) x else cli::cli_abort(errmsg), schemas)
  
  # proceed to read the parquet files one by one
  cli::cli_progress_bar(name = "Reading parquet files", total = length(pq_files))
  cli::cli_progress_update(set = 0, force = TRUE)
  df <- read_parquet(pq_files[1], col_select = col_select, options = options)
  cli::cli_progress_update(1, force = TRUE)
  for (i in 2:length(pq_files)) {
    df <- dplyr::bind_rows(df, read_parquet(pq_files[i], col_select = col_select, options = options))
    cli::cli_progress_update(1)
  }
  cli::cli_progress_done()
  df
}
```

Which can read the above situation like so and provides nice progress bars:

```R
df <- read_parquet_glob("disease_database_v1.0/**/*.parquet")
```

title: Write metadata only
description:
We have a use case for a survey I'm involved with using Parquet where we want to write a small amount amount of survey specific metadata (using our asgr/MAML-format) to a specific part of an existing Parquet file's metadata (not the column schema part of course).

Using R/arrow it seems the only way to do this involves a full streamed copy of the binary data (slow, since the file is 100GB). Since nanoparquet supports a write only append mode, I was wondering if it might be possible via a similar mechanism? A bit of ggging suggests this is possible with the lower level C++ API, not not the current R/arrow or pyarrow (or nanoparquet?) packages. Thoughts very much appreciated, and I'm happy to go into more detail about why we are doing this if needed (but maybe the link to the MAML repo makes it somewhat clear- we need richer metadata in astronomy).

Thanks, and also- great work with nanoparquet! It's helped us already in some JupyterHub environments where arrow was tricky to build.

title: Unexpected result when writing `bit64::as.integer64()` type
description:
The following reprex compares writing a column of type `bit64::integer64()` into a parquet file using {arrow} and using {nanoparquet}. nanoparquet seems to either write or read wrong values, but without an explicit error message:

``` r
df <-
  tibble::tibble(
    x = bit64::as.integer64(1000),
    y = 1000L
  )

npar <- withr::local_tempfile()
apar <- withr::local_tempfile()

nanoparquet::write_parquet(df, npar)
nanoparquet::read_parquet(npar)
#> # A data frame: 1 × 2
#>           x     y
#>       <dbl> <int>
#> 1 4.94e-321  1000

options(arrow.int64_downcast = FALSE)
arrow::write_parquet(df, apar)
arrow::read_parquet(apar)
#> # A tibble: 1 × 2
#>         x     y
#>   <int64> <int>
#> 1    1000  1000
```

<sup>Created on 2026-01-29 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

I'd propose to either add support for `bit64::as.integer64()` type, or at least provide an error when encountering the type, so the user knows that this is not supported.

title: Minor update to documentation
description:
For "other tools": Polars, Python's equivalent to data.table but with more tidy-like syntax, directly supports parquet including "lazy" operations.

For limitations: This may be parquet in general but loading a parquet file in Arrow keeps it locked somehow. Attempting to write to that same file from python while the dataframe exists in R causes problems. Sometimes the lock is so bad I need to `rm()` the file in R, force a garbage collect, and then delete the parquet file to get new data loading into R again.

If nanoparquet doesn't have this limitation that would be a very significant improvement in QOL, if it does it's worth mentioning.

description:

### Simplified benchmarking
```

nanoparquet::read_parquet(file_name)
```

## Further findings

After some trial and errors, I made some discoveries:

1) Not all method of compression generated the same error:
		a) snappy: ```Couldn't deserialize thrift: don't know what type:```
		b) zstd: ```Couldn't deserialize thrift: TProtocolException: Invalid data```
		c) uncompressed : ```Couldn't deserialize thrift: TProtocolException: Invalid data```
		d) gzip: no error. The script worked

2) The machine has more than enough memory:
		a) There is space available on disk: ```df -h``` showed 783GB free
		b) Same story for the RAM: 472GB shows as total by running ```free -g``` with over 90% not allocated

3) Creating a minimal working example didn't work: creating 100 datasets with 10M rows by cycling the RNG seed and on each of them running  ```write_parquet``` with ```compress = "uncompressed"``` didn't raise any error

4) Running ```write_parquet``` on columns ```b, c, d``` did not work; however, on each pair subset of the previous triplet the script works ```((b, c), (c, d), (b, d))```


6) Files unopenable to nanoparquet are also unopenable by polars. The script errors out with:

``` parquet: File out of specification: Invalid thrift: protocol error```

## Closing remarks

Taking into account everything, the problem is probably related to writing large datasets however I couldn't pinpoint the location of the issues or a solution to it

title: FR: Make read_parquet tibble of class tbl_df
description:
Following a comment in #104:

> I wonder why the default value of class is `c("tbl", "data.frame")` and not `c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")`? It seems to me that `tbl` is more of an "interface" than a class, since all actual instances of `tbl`s that I have encountered previously are actually also other classes such as either `tbl_df` or more complex types (such as those found in `dbplyr`). And the returned object is structurally a `tbl_df`, right, so it would be useful for any functions taking it to be able to use the most specific class information?

I arrived here because of this:

``` r
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = "parquet")

tibble::tibble(a = 1) |>
  nanoparquet::write_parquet(tmp)

df <- nanoparquet::read_parquet(tmp)

class(df)
#> [1] "tbl"        "data.frame"
class(tibble::as_tibble(df))
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"

df |>
  dplyr::summarise() |>
  class()
#> [1] "data.frame"

df |>
  tibble::as_tibble() |>
  dplyr::summarise() |>
  class()
#> [1] "tbl_df"     "tbl"        "data.frame"
```

<sup>Created on 2025-07-16 with [reprex v2.1.1](https://reprex.tidyverse.org)</sup>

Functions like `dplyr::summarise()` use `tibble::is_tibble()` internally to check whether something is a tibble, but this is checking specifically on class `tbl_df`, not `tbl`. Since this check gives `FALSE`, the tibble is silently converted to a raw `data.frame`.

Is there any reason why the object returned by `read_parquet()` doesn't have the more specific `tbl_df` class? If it did have it, situations like the one I described would be clearer and less error prone, i.e., users wouldn't have to manually add this class with `tibble::as_tibble()`.

title: `class` does not work in `read_parquet()`
description:
> Apologies for (possibly) submitting a support request disguised as an issue report, but I am failing to get the `class` option to work and can't figure out what is going wrong. Here is the `reprex`:> 
> > 
> ``` r> 
> # Load nanoparquet> 
> library(nanoparquet)> 
> packageVersion("nanoparquet")> 
> #> [1] '0.3.1.9000'> 
> > 
> # Write a data.frame> 
> d <- data.frame(letters)> 
> f <- tempfile()> 
> write_parquet(d, f)> 
> > 
> # Read after setting options> 
> options(nanoparquet.class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))> 
> read_parquet(f) |> class()> 
> #> [1] "tbl"        "data.frame"> 
> > 
> # Read using explicit parquet_options()> 
> read_parquet(f, options = parquet_options(class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))) |> class()> 
> #> [1] "tbl"        "data.frame"> 
> > 
> # Try alternative specifications> 
> read_parquet(f, options = parquet_options(class = c("data.frame")))    |> class()> 
> #> [1] "tbl"        "data.frame"> 
> read_parquet(f, options = parquet_options(class = character()))        |> class()> 
> #> [1] "tbl"        "data.frame"> 
> read_parquet(f, options = parquet_options(class = "tbl_df"))           |> class()> 
> #> [1] "tbl"        "data.frame"> 
> read_parquet(f, options = parquet_options(class = ""))                 |> class()> 
> #> [1] "tbl"        "data.frame"> 
> ```> 
> > 
> A few other somewhat related thoughts:> 
> > 
> - I appreciate the concern that one does not want to restore a broken object. One possibility for allowing the storage of different types of data frames would be to have an `accept_classes` (or simply `classes`) parameter, which would only allow reading (and writing?) objects if any classes were included in the `accept_classes` list, punting the responsibility to the user. Trying to read/write objects with unlisted class entries would result in an error. A default value of `c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")` would allow some very common use cases (i.e. base data frames and tibbles) to be transparently round-tripped. Interaction with `class` could work by some heuristic about priorities, such as:> 
>   - On write, add class data if `accept_classes` is set> 
>   - On read, if `accept_classes` is set and class data is found when reading a parquet file, use that> 
>   - If no class data is found when reading a parquet file, use value from `class`> 
>   - If one or the other params are `null`/`NA`, use the other> 
>   - If both are `null`/`NA`, error out> 
> - Would it make sense to reserve `...` as the first parameter in `parquet_options()` to force the use of name-based parameters and prevent location-based usage? It feels like `parquet_options()` might accumulate a lot of parameters over time, and having the flexibility to group related parameters would help with documentation, but reordering them would break existing location-based usage. Putting `...` first would of course break backwards compatibility now, but ensure that later reordering of parameters would from then on be backwards compatible. Since it is still early days for `nanoparquet` I think it might be worthwhile trade-off.> 
> - I wonder why the default value of `class` is `c("tbl", "data.frame")` and not `c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")`? It seems to me that `tbl` is more of an "interface" than a class, since all actual instances of `tbl`s  that I have encountered previously are actually also other classes such as either `tbl_df` or more complex types (such as those found in `dbplyr`). And the returned object is structurally a `tbl_df`, right, so it would be useful for any functions taking it to be able to use the most specific class information?

title: Timezone is ignored during I/O operations
description:
I've just noticed some unexpected behaviour with POSIXct data types. The timezone argument is completely ignored by `nanoparquet` during both `read_parquet` and `write_parquet` operations. Below is a small reprex showing a comparison in behaviour between `nanoparquet` and `arrow` packages. As you can see `arrow::write_parquet` acknowledges the timezone, while `nanoparquet::write_parquet` drops it to defaults (UTC in my case).

Interestingly, the Parquet file, even when written with `arrow::write_parquet`, also cannot read the timezone when opened with `nanoparquet::read_parquet`, whereas `arrow::read_parquet` reads it as expected.

```r
library(dplyr)
library(lubridate)
library(nanoparquet)
library(arrow)

set.seed(123)
df <-
storms |>
dplyr::slice_sample(n = 1000) |>
dplyr::mutate(
  name,
  datetime = lubridate::make_datetime(year,month,day,hour,tz = "UTC"),
  datetime_tz = lubridate::with_tz(datetime, "America/New_York"),
  .keep = "none"
)

# Compare timezones
waldo::compare(
  lubridate::tz(df$datetime),
  lubridate::tz(df$datetime_tz)
)
#> `old`: "UTC"             
#> `new`: "America/New_York"

# {nanoparquet} approach
tmp_nano <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
nanoparquet::write_parquet(df, tmp_nano)

df_nano <- nanoparquet::read_parquet(tmp_nano)

waldo::compare(
  lubridate::tz(df_nano$datetime),
  lubridate::tz(df_nano$datetime_tz)
)
#> ✔ No differences

# {arrow} approach
tmp_arrow <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
arrow::write_parquet(df, tmp_arrow)
df_arrow <- arrow::read_parquet(tmp_arrow)

waldo::compare(
  lubridate::tz(df_arrow$datetime),
  lubridate::tz(df_arrow$datetime_tz)
)
#> `old`: "UTC"             
#> `new`: "America/New_York"

# Read parquet file written with {nanoparquet} using {arrow}
arrow::read_parquet(tmp_nano) |>
  dplyr::pull(datetime_tz) |>
  lubridate::tz() # Should be America/New_York
#> [1] "UTC"

# Read parquet file written with {arrow} using {nanoparquet}
nanoparquet::read_parquet(tmp_arrow) |>
  dplyr::pull(datetime_tz) |>
  lubridate::tz() # Should be America/New_York
#> [1] "UTC"
```

When I repeatedly read a file, the `raw` version of the data is different almost every time.

As an example, here I repeatedly read a file. It contains a column `aggregated_numerator`, which is logical. Thus, it should have at most two distinct values.

When I do this with `arrow`, there are always two distinct values.
When I do it with `nanoparquet` there are sometimes 2, sometimes 3, sometimes, 58, etc, etc.

When I print the distinct values, they look like `FALSE`, `TRUE`, `TRUE`, `TRUE`, etc. This is unusual because I would expect all of the `TRUE` values to be non-distinct.

If I call `as.raw` on these values, we see that they are actually different. This causes strange issues when checking the truth value later.

I have uploaded the file [here](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1ZpRo75DAkZUBGHeHttvacq3ump5Rh-6S/view?usp=share_link).

```r
> my_path <- "example.parquet"
> n <- 5
> x <- purrr::map(1:n, \(x) nanoparquet::read_parquet(my_path))
> y <- purrr::map(1:n, \(x) arrow::read_parquet(my_path))
> 
> ## aggregated_numerator is supposed to lgl, so there should be at most 2 distinct values
> uniques_x <- purrr::map_int(x, \(z) dplyr::n_distinct(z$aggregated_numerator))
> uniques_y <- purrr::map_int(y, \(z) dplyr::n_distinct(z$aggregated_numerator))
> 
> uniques_x # nanoparquet is weird
[1]  3 58 17 58 58
> uniques_y # arrow is fine
[1] 2 2 2 2 2
> 
> # Investigate nanoparquet weirdness
> bad_ex <- which(uniques_x != 2)[1]
> 
> bad_vals <-  x[[bad_ex]] |> 
+   dplyr::distinct(aggregated_numerator) |> 
+   dplyr::pull()
> 
> bad_vals
[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE
> 
> as.raw(bad_vals)
[1] 00 01 b9
> 
> purrr::map_lgl(bad_vals, isTRUE)
[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE
> 
> vctrs::vec_equal(bad_vals, TRUE)
[1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE
```

title: FR: concatenate existing parquet files
description:
Similar to `append_parquet`, but accept one or more existing parquet files on disk, writing to a file on disk (perhaps new?).

While this might be useful as an addition to `append_parquet`, I think its use-case is specific enough to justify its own function.

Use-case: I have a "datamart" where top-level subdirectories indicate the specific table/schema to follow, then subdirs under those are hive-partitioned. Each bottom-level directory contains one or more `.pq` files that are read in using `arrow::open_dataset`.  Current methodology adds a new parquet file when new data is made available, mostly for two reasons: (1) `append_parquet` didn't exist when I wrote it, and (2) the frequency of new-data can be multiple/minute or days-between-new-data, so it seemed simplest to work with multiple-pq-files.

However ... as expected, once the number of files exceeds some level, the overhead of evaluating schema/metadata gets more expensive, so we want to compact the data existing in those pq files into a single pq file. The current method for this is rather memory-heavy, as it reads everything into memory all at once.

Using the new `append_metadata` (not tested, I just learned of this today), my first attempt would be to copy the first pq file to a temp-file (since it is not atomic), then read-and-append each file after that. This may be faster or at least no-slower and more memory-efficient than reading all of the pq files into memory at once (some of these collections have 10Mi rows among the pq files).

But it could be much much better (faster) if the data concatenation were done closer to the data, not in "R".

Thoughts?

title: mention remote access in limitations?
description:
this is a cool project.  In the limitations, it is worth mentioning that this package isn't intended to support remote range request of parquet files either, e.g. from S3 or https, which both the `arrow` (for S3) and `duckdb` (on all protocols) packages support.  

Notably (and as you probably already know) at the moment, the Mac binaries on CRAN for arrow don't support S3, (though historically they have and the r-universe ones do), and so users may mistakenly think this provides an alternative.  The limitations section doesn't mention this but also doesn't give any indication that it is not an exhaustive list.  Especially as this package is obviously targeted at non-experts, I think this is worth clearly documenting.  

Also just a side comment, but I think duckdb is already particularly smooth for most users to install, and avoids setting up the confusion down the road when limitations of nanoparquet matter. Read & write factors?
description:
Arrow writes factors as `dictionary<values=string, indices=int32>`, so we should probably do the same.

miniparquet currently reads that dictionary as a string column, so we'd need to change that as well.

In Python, Pandas uses pyarrow to read/write parquet files by default, but if pyarrow is not installed, it falls back to fastparquet. 

pyarrow reads in `dictionary<values=string, indices=int32>` as a `category` in Pandas, and then writes it back to `dictionary<values=string, indices=int32>` correctly. So this is good.

fastparquet reads in `dictionary<values=string, indices=int32>` as `object`, but AFAICT it is just a list of strings. Then it'll write it back as strings. So this is not so good.

duckdb also reads in `dictionary<values=string, indices=int32>` as a sting column. When writing a factor into a duckdb database, it actually keeps it a factor. But then when we write the DB table to parquet, it converts it to string.
